title: Top N senders with alphabetical tie-break
problem: A chat service wants a 'most active senders' list. Implement top_senders(messages, n) in ranking.py: count each sender's messages, ignoring messages with empty text, then return the names of the top n senders, most messages first, with ties broken alphabetically. n is how many names to return. It is not a message count.
requirements: Count messages per sender; a message with text == "" doesn't count
Rank senders by message count, highest first
Break ties in count alphabetically by name (A to Z)
Return at most n names: the first n of that ranking, or all of them if there are fewer
contract: top_senders(messages: list[tuple[str, str]], n: int) -> list[str]
expectedBehavior: With ali 3 messages, bob 2, sara 1: n=1 -> ['ali'], n=2 -> ['ali', 'bob'], n=3 or more -> ['ali', 'bob', 'sara']. With kian 2, tara 1, dana 1 and n=2 -> ['kian', 'dana'].
edgeCases: Ties whose input order is not alphabetical
A tie exactly at the cutoff (who gets the last place?)
n larger than the number of senders
Senders whose only messages are empty strings don't appear at all
The caller's list must be unchanged afterwards
hints: Conceptual: this is three steps, in order: count (a dict of name -> count), rank (one sorted call whose key encodes both rules), cut (take the first n). Counter.most_common alone is not enough, because it breaks ties by first appearance, not alphabetically.

Specific: the sort key for a sender must make higher counts sort first and, among equal counts, names sort A to Z. A tuple key does both; reverse=True does not (it would flip the names too). Taking the first n with a slice is safe even when n is larger than the number of senders.
Implementation: validate n first. Loop over the (sender, text) pairs and count only when text is non-empty. Then sort the senders with key=lambda s: (-count_of_s, s) and return the slice up to n.
evaluation: One sorted() call with a tuple key; no hand-written sorting loop
Uses sorted() (new list), not .sort() on the caller's data
Tested mentally against a tie at the cutoff before running pytest
